rewriteLast.title: Chapter 6 · Making Ready
rewriteLast.artPrompt: three children tidying a small cottage parlour in pale winter light, a boy sweeping, a girl polishing a chair, another girl beating a pillow by an open window, an open telegram lying on the table between them, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The next morning the children woke early, and the winter sun was bright. All their hearts were full of one thing. Father was coming home! But Mother, when they asked when, shook her head gently. "The telegram says he is coming," she said. "The old gentleman's lawyers must first finish making his name quite clean. It will take a little time. So we shall keep well and busy, and be glad."

So they began to make the house ready. Peter swept and carried, and Phyllis polished everything that would stand still. Bobbie aired the little room at the back, and beat the pillow till the feathers flew. "He will want to see the railway first thing," said Peter. "No," said Phyllis, "he will want his supper first thing." And they laughed, because even waiting is easier when you talk about it.
Three children tidy the parlour, with the telegram lying open on the table between them.

One evening Bobbie went to her mother and put her arms round her. "Mother," she said, "I read the paper. I know what they said about Father. I have known for a long time, and I never told, because it would have hurt you." Mother held her close for a long minute. "You are the bravest of us all," she said. "And now we are all brave together, which is the best way."
Question for you: The children know Father is coming home, but not on which day. What would you do to make a house ready for someone you love?

And so, while the great men in London worked slowly at Father's case, life went on. The Railway Children went on being the Railway Children. There were trains to wave to, and gardens to weed, and washing to help with, and coal to fetch. The days were full, and the nights were quiet. The winter turned slowly into spring. And every day the 9:15 went by, carrying their love to London.

chapters.title: Chapter 7 · The Man at the Station
chapters.artPrompt: a tall ragged traveller with a pale sad face sitting hunched on a wooden station bench, a girl in a straw hat offering him bread, a boy and a smaller girl watching from beside a luggage trolley, warm summer afternoon light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: It was a hot July day, and the children went down to the station for a picnic by the cutting. They carried bread and butter with them. The 9:15 came in, and went on. And then, from the back of a slow goods train, a man climbed stiffly down. He was tall, in ragged foreign clothes, with a pale face and sad dark eyes. He looked about him like a man waking from a long, bad dream.

He spoke to the porters, but it was no language they knew. He sat down on a bench, and put his head in his hands. He did not seem to see anyone at all. He was hungry, and he was alone. Then Bobbie did a Bobbie thing. She went up to him and held out the picnic bread, and smiled. The man took it, and looked at her, and two tears ran down his brown face.
A ragged stranger with sad dark eyes sits on a station bench, a girl offering him bread.

Peter fetched the station-master, and Phyllis filled the man's cap with cool water from the tap. Nobody could understand a word he said. The station-master looked at him kindly too. But the children understood the hungry way he ate, and the shaking of his hands. He looked again and again at the three of them, as if he were counting them. "We shall take him home to Mother," said Bobbie. "Mother always knows what to do."
New word: foreign - from a far-away country, with different clothes and words. This man's words were all foreign, but his hunger and his sadness were plain.

So they walked him gently up the hill. Peter went on one side, and Bobbie on the other, and Phyllis carried the bread. And Mother met them at the gate of Three Chimneys, and saw everything in one look. "Bring him in," she said. "The spare room, and hot water, and no questions till he has slept."

chapters.title: Chapter 8 · The Prisoner's Story
chapters.artPrompt: a grey-eyed traveller in borrowed clothes telling a story by a cottage fire, his hands drawing shapes of snow and iron bars in the air, a mother and three children listening close in the firelight, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The stranger slept for nearly two days. When he woke he was calmer. He tried to thank them in his own tongue, and in broken French, and with his hands. Mother could speak a little French, luckily. And between them, slowly, the story came out, like something heavy being pulled up from a well.

He was a writer, he said, in a great cold country where the ruler did not like the truth. He had written a book - only a book, only words - but the words were true. For them he had been taken away to a prison in the ice and snow, far from everyone he loved. He had been a prisoner for years and years. When at last they let him go, his wife and children had fled to England. He crossed half of Europe on foot to find them.
The grey-eyed traveller tells his story by the fire, his hands drawing shapes of snow and iron bars.

"A prisoner," said Peter, trying the word. "For writing a true book." The children looked at the tall, bent man, and thought of Father in his prison. He too was shut up for nothing. Something went out from them to him that needed no language at all. That night they wrote to the old gentleman, and told him the whole story, and asked him to help.
New word: prisoner - someone kept locked up against their will. The children knew that word already, in a quiet, aching way.

And the old gentleman answered by return of post. If the man was the writer he believed him to be, then his name was honoured in every library. And his family - his family should be found. "Leave it to me," the old gentleman wrote. So they left it to him, and hoped. All the same, the writer watched the trains from the window like a man watching a door.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 · The Family Found
chapters.artPrompt: a reunited family meeting in the middle of a cottage flower garden with arms out wide, a pale lady and three children running to a beaming tall man, three English children watching from the gate, bright summer morning, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Letters went out from the old gentleman to people whose business is helping people, and three long weeks passed. Then, one bright morning, a carriage came up the hill to Three Chimneys. The children were at the gate before it stopped. Out of it stepped a pale lady in black, and three children. They were a boy and two girls, with dark hair and their father's same sad eyes.

The writer was in the garden, planting beans, because Mother said that idle hands worry. He looked up, and stood quite still, and the beans fell out of his hands. Nobody spoke. Then he went across the grass with his arms out. The lady ran, and the children ran. The whole family met in the middle of the garden, like one thing coming back to itself. Even Peter, who does not cry, blew his nose twice.
A family meets in the middle of a cottage garden with arms out, the summer flowers trodden and forgotten.

The lady kissed Mother's hands, and could not stop. A friend said the words for her. Her husband had told her of three children with bread, and of a mother with kind eyes. The children were kissed too, many, many times, and did not mind it a bit. "In my country," the lady said, "we say that some strangers are sent by heaven. I say that yours were sent by their own good hearts."
Talk together: the writer lost everything, and the children helped him find it again. Ask your child: what would you give to help a stranger who had lost his family?

The Russian family found a little house of their own on the far side of the village. The writer planted a garden at once. In it he put a bench, set just where you could see the railway. "So I remember," he said. And often on fine summer days, the two gardens sent flowers to each other by small running messengers.

chapters.title: Chapter 10 · Bobbie's Ride
chapters.artPrompt: a girl in a beribboned hat standing inside the cab of a great green steam engine, steam curling round a smiling driver's cap, a boy and a smaller girl waving from the platform, bright morning light on shining rails, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Ever since the day of the red petticoats, the express driver had counted the children among his friends. One bright morning he saw them on the platform and beckoned. "We've a clean engine and a light load today," he said. "How would your Mother feel about one of her children riding in a real engine, proper and all?"

Mother said yes, for the driver was a careful man with kind eyes. So Bobbie climbed the iron steps into the cab. Peter and Phyllis watched from the platform, sick with pride and envy in equal parts. Her heart hammered like the pistons, and she stood as straight as a flagstaff. The driver put his hand on the regulator. "Now then, missy," he said. "You shall see what an engine can do when she's asked nicely."
A girl in a beribboned hat stands in the cab of a great green engine, steam curling round the driver's smile.

The world began to run. Hedges flicked past like green ribbons, and the telegraph wires sang. The big wheels beat their steady song upon the rail. Bobbie saw Three Chimneys flash by on its hill, and the cutting where the petticoats had flown. She waved and waved, though nobody down there could see her. She was riding an engine. She was riding an engine, and it was better than dreaming.
New word: regulator - the lever an engine driver moves to let steam to the wheels and start the train.

At the far station the driver lifted her down. The fireman shook her hand as if she were grown up. "You kept your head well," he said. "That is what engine folk do." Bobbie walked home through the fields feeling about a foot taller. Peter talked of nothing else for a week, and made a drawing of the regulator that nobody could understand. It is a fine thing, Bobbie thought, to be trusted by an engine.

chapters.title: Chapter 11 · Jim Gets Well
chapters.artPrompt: a cheerful boy with his leg strapped straight lying propped on pillows by a cottage window, three friends around him acting out a story, a steam train passing beyond the glass, bright afternoon light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Jim's broken leg mended slowly, in the little room at the back with the window on the railway. All day the trains went by his window. The children told him their private names for every one of them. Jim was the grandson of the old gentleman. He was brave and funny, and he learned to whistle like a train before he could walk like a boy. Jim learned all their games, and they learned his. Before long, Three Chimneys would not have seemed right without him.

He told them about his school, and his grandfather's big quiet house. Grandfather and grandson, he said, were all the family each other had. "He is the best man in the world," said Jim. "We know someone else who is," said Bobbie, and looked at the door where Mother stood. Jim said no more, but he understood.
A boy with a strapped leg lies propped by a window, three friends around him, a train beyond the glass.

At last the day came when Jim could walk to the station on two sticks. Then he walked on one, and then on his own two feet. Peter circled him like a proud mother hen. The old gentleman came down from London to fetch him, and stayed to tea. He praised the garden, and said nothing at all about Father. But his eyes were kind, and Bobbie understood the nothing.
Talk together: the children made Jim's long weeks of getting well feel short. Ask your child: what would you do to cheer a friend who must stay in bed?

The last they saw of him, Jim was waving from the carriage window with both hands. He was shouting that he would come back for the haymaking. He said that next time he would keep out of tunnels. The train ran him away to London, to school, and to his grandfather's house. But he came back, more than once, always. And he never once brought the same present twice.

chapters.title: Chapter 12 · The Signal Box
chapters.artPrompt: the inside of a bright railway signal box with rows of polished brass levers, two children sitting on a bench by a little iron stove, a signal-man pointing out of the window at signals marching down the line, storybook illustration

blocks.text: There was no better place in the world, Peter said, than the signal box. The signal-man almost agreed with him. The children were allowed in, two at a time, to sit still and watch by the little stove. Levers of polished brass rose from the floor in rows. When the great levers swung, the whole box seemed to breathe. Each one moved a signal far down the line.

The signal-man showed them how the bells spoke to the next box along the line. One beat meant a goods train, and two meant a passenger, and so on. "The railway's all one family," he said. "Box tells box, and station tells station, and every train is watched till she's safe past." The children thought that was like their family too, waiting for one missing man.
Inside a bright signal box, two children sit by a little stove among rows of brass levers.

One wild afternoon they watched a storm walk up the valley. It bent the trees, and chased white water down the cutting. The signal-man stood at the window with his tea forgotten. The children held their breath as the expresses fought through. Phyllis said afterwards that the thunder made her heart fly up like a bird. Not one single train was late enough to matter. "Good line," said the signal-man, "and good folk on it." And he gave them each a piece of shortbread.
New word: signal - a moving arm on a tall post that tells the driver whether the line ahead is clear. Red means stop, and never forget it.

Walking home in the wet dusk, they saw the signal lamp glowing red against the rain. It was steady as a promise. "Everything on the railway points somewhere," said Bobbie. "Signals point the way, and rails point to London." And the 9:15 thundered by below them, windows lit and warm. It carried strangers towards their own homes, and their love towards Father.

chapters.title: Chapter 13 · Waiting and Working
chapters.artPrompt: three children on a wet autumn railway bank waving handkerchiefs at the lit windows of the London train as it thunders past in the rain, bare trees and a distant white cottage, soft grey light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The summer ripened into autumn, and the waiting went on. The children learned the great lesson of waiting: keep your hands busy. Mother's stories came out in magazines, and there was bread-and-cheese for tea, and sometimes jam. The garden was dug over for winter, and the apples were stored in straw under the bed. Peter made a wheelbarrow with a broken wheel that went to one side. Everyone used it and praised it, and nobody minded the side it went to.

Perks taught them to read the railway like a book. They learned the meaning of every whistle, and the smell of rain on rails. They learned the sound of a wheel that wanted looking at. Bobbie sewed her own frock and Phyllis's, and dropped stitches, and picked them up again. And every single morning, whatever the weather, three hands waved to the 9:15 from the bank.
Three children on a wet autumn bank wave at the lit windows of the 9:15 as it thunders past.

Once a week the old gentleman's letter came, always with the same ending: "Working hard for you. Be of good courage." Once a week Mother read it aloud. Once a week they pretended not to watch her face. Nobody said Father's name much, but everybody thought it. Nobody quite lost heart. But Phyllis cried over a dropped egg one morning, and Mother pretended not to see that either.
Question for you: The children keep waving at the 9:15 even when waiting is hard. Why do you think the waving matters so much to them?

Then, on a white and frosty morning, came a knock. It was Perks, taking off his cap before he reached the door. "A letter, missis - special delivery," he said. "And I brought it myself, because I could see it was welcome by the look of the envelope." Mother read it once in silence. Then she called the children in, and her voice was shaking, and it was shaking with joy.

chapters.title: Chapter 14 · The Name Made Clean
chapters.artPrompt: a firelit cottage parlour made ready for a homecoming with a lavender tablecloth, a mended armchair and plates set out, three children rushing about with a bucket of coals and a whitewash brush, winter evening light through the window, storybook illustration

blocks.text: "Children," Mother said, "Father's name is made quite clean. The great men have proved it was all a mistake, and the papers are signed. He is free." For a moment nobody moved. Then Phyllis began to jump up and down. Peter let out a whoop like a train whistle. And Bobbie stood quite still, and let the happiness come, like standing in warm rain.

There was so much to do. The little back room was whitewashed again, though it had been done before. Phyllis carried hot coals up to the spare room in a bucket, and only spilled them twice. The chair by the fire was mended where its arm had cracked. Mother's best tablecloth came out of its paper, smelling of lavender. Peter saved his pocket money, both pence of it. He bought a pipe cleaner, because Father smoked a pipe. Phyllis learned to make scones, which nobody at all regretted.
A firelit parlour made ready with a lavender tablecloth and a mended armchair, three children setting out plates.

The old gentleman wrote that he would come to the station too. He would stand quietly at the back, where Father could see him. "I have waited for this day as long as any of you," he wrote. "And longer than most, for I grew fond of you all before I knew whose children you were." Bobbie read that part twice.
New word: whitewash - a white paint washed on walls to make them clean and bright. This one was happiness itself.

The day before, they walked down to the station just to look at the rails. They shone away towards London like two roads of silver. "Suppose the train is late," said Phyllis. "Trains are never late that matter," said Peter. "It will be tomorrow," Bobbie said to herself. "Tomorrow, tomorrow." But she only looked down the line a long time, and her heart was too full for timetables.

chapters.title: Chapter 15 · Father Comes Home
chapters.artPrompt: a tall thin man stepping down from a London train onto a small misty platform, a girl flying to him with open arms past startled passengers, a mother and two children running close behind, an old gentleman watching kindly under the station clock, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The day came, grey and sweet, with smoke standing straight up from the chimneys. The children were on the platform an hour too soon. Perks contrived to be sweeping the same spot the whole time. Everybody watched the line, where the smoke would come from. The old gentleman stood at the back under the clock, as he had written. Mother came down at the last minute, very pale, holding Bobbie's hand very tight.

Then, far down the line, a thread of smoke, and the singing of the rails. The London train came in slowly, breathing like a great tired animal. Doors opened and shut, and people stepped down with bags and umbrellas. The children's eyes went from one to another, and none of them was Father. And then, from the first-class carriage, a tall thin man stepped down, and Bobbie's heart stopped, and then thundered. "FATHER! Oh! FATHER!"
A tall thin man steps down from a London train, a girl flying to him along the platform.

He had her up in his arms before she reached him. Peter and Phyllis were there the next moment, and then Mother. The family was one thing again, right there among the suitcases. The porters looked another way. Perks found something urgent to do with his broom. He wiped his eyes with the back of his hand when nobody was watching.
Question for you: All through the story, the children waved their love to London on the 9:15. How do you think Father knew they would be on that platform?

They walked home the long way, over the bridge and past the cutting. Father said he wanted to see everything. He carried Phyllis on his shoulder until she was too big, which took some time. And the smoke of Three Chimneys rose to meet them, and the kettle was put on. The 9:15 went by at its proper minute. Nobody waved at all, because the reason for the waving was walking home with them.
